---
title: "Get started"
---

This guide installs Positron Server on an HPC cluster and adds a Positron tile
to Open OnDemand (OOD). You do four things: install Positron Server where the
compute nodes can read it, place the license file, install this app on the OOD
host, and check that the OOD reverse proxy is on. Then you launch a session and
run the [test checklist](test_checklist.qmd).

The guide installs Positron Server directly on a shared filesystem, which is
the shortest path to a first session. If your site runs interactive apps from
Apptainer images, do Steps 1 and 2 inside an image instead, then continue
with Step 3. [Run inside Apptainer](configuration.qmd#run-inside-apptainer)
covers the image.

## Before you start

You need:

- An OOD host on OOD 3.0 or newer, with a Slurm cluster defined in
  `/etc/ood/config/clusters.d/`. The app uses Slurm `sbatch` options.
- Root access on the OOD host, and write access to a filesystem that every
  compute node mounts, such as `/opt` or an applications directory.
- A Positron Server license file (`license.lic`) from Posit. Positron Server
  refuses to start in a hosted environment without a license.
- At least 2.5 GB of RAM per session on the compute nodes.
- Compute nodes with glibc 2.34 or newer and OpenSSL 3, for example RHEL 9,
  Rocky Linux 9, or Ubuntu 22.04 or newer. The `license-manager` binary that
  checks the license file needs both.

The compute nodes also need the `shuf` command and `ss` or `lsof`, which OOD
uses to find a free port. Standard Linux distributions have them.

## Step 1: Install Positron Server {#install-positron-server}

Positron Server is available only as a Linux archive from the Posit content
delivery network (CDN). It does not appear on the Positron download page or on
the GitHub releases page. Download the build that matches the CPU architecture
of your compute nodes:

| Architecture | Download |
|---|---|
| x86_64 (Intel and AMD) | [positron-server-linux-x64-{{< var positron.version >}}.tar.gz]({{< var positron.url-x64 >}}) |
| ARM64 | [positron-server-linux-arm64-{{< var positron.version >}}.tar.gz]({{< var positron.url-arm64 >}}) |

Unpack it into a directory that every compute node can read. This guide uses
`/opt/positron-server`. To download and unpack from the command line, run the
commands for your architecture as root, on a host that mounts that directory.

**For x86_64:**

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
CDN=https://cdn.posit.co/positron/releases/server
curl -L -o /tmp/positron-server.tar.gz \
  "$CDN/x86_64/positron-server-linux-x64-{{< var positron.version >}}.tar.gz"
mkdir -p /opt/positron-server
tar -xzf /tmp/positron-server.tar.gz -C /opt/positron-server \
  --strip-components=1
```

**For ARM64:**

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
CDN=https://cdn.posit.co/positron/releases/server
curl -L -o /tmp/positron-server.tar.gz \
  "$CDN/arm64/positron-server-linux-arm64-{{< var positron.version >}}.tar.gz"
mkdir -p /opt/positron-server
tar -xzf /tmp/positron-server.tar.gz -C /opt/positron-server \
  --strip-components=1
```

Confirm the install from a compute node, not from the OOD host:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
/opt/positron-server/bin/positron-server --version
```

In Step 3 you tell the app where this directory is. If your site provides
software through environment modules, you can make a module for Positron
Server and name that module in Step 3 instead. See
[Install location](configuration.qmd#install-location).

## Step 2: Place the license file {#place-the-license-file}

Posit sends the license file to you directly. It is a small text file that
starts with `-----BEGIN RSTUDIO LICENSE-----`, and its name varies.

Copy it into the activation directory, next to the bundled `license-manager`
binary, with the name `license.lic`. In the command below, replace
`/path/to/your-license.lic` with the file you received, and `<arch>` with
`x86_64` or `aarch64`:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
install -m 644 /path/to/your-license.lic \
  /opt/positron-server/resources/activation/linux/<arch>/license.lic
```

The license file needs mode `644`. Each session runs `positron-server` as the
user who launched it, and `positron-server` reads the license file itself.
With a root-only mode such as `600`, every session fails to start. This also
means that every user who can start a session can read the file. See
[License file location](configuration.qmd#license-file-location) for what
that implies and for the alternative.

Before you continue, confirm that `license-manager` accepts the license file.
Run this on a compute node, or on any host with the same architecture:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
/opt/positron-server/resources/activation/linux/<arch>/license-manager status
```

The output reports `activated` or `evaluation` and the days left. If the
install directory is read-only, or several clusters share one install, see
[License file location](configuration.qmd#license-file-location) for other
places to put the file.

## Step 3: Install the app {#install-the-app}

On the OOD host, clone this repository into the system apps directory:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
cd /var/www/ood/apps/sys
git clone https://github.com/posit-dev/positron-server-ood.git positron
```

Then open `/var/www/ood/apps/sys/positron/form.yml` and set the site settings
at the top of the file:

```{.yaml filename="form.yml"}
cluster: "hpc"

attributes:
  positron_server_dir: "/opt/positron-server"
  positron_module: ""
  apptainer_image: ""
  apptainer_binds: ""
```

- `cluster` is the file name, without `.yml`, of your cluster in
  `/etc/ood/config/clusters.d/`.
- `positron_server_dir` is the directory from Step 1. Leave it empty if
  `positron-server` is already on `PATH` on the compute nodes.
- Leave the other three empty for a plain install.
  [Configuration](configuration.qmd) describes them.

OOD reads the app directory on each request. You do not restart anything after
you install or edit the app.

## Step 4: Turn on the reverse proxy {#turn-on-the-reverse-proxy}

OOD connects the browser to the session through its reverse proxy. The app uses
the `/rnode/` path, which is off by default. In `/etc/ood/config/ood_portal.yml`,
set:

```{.yaml filename="/etc/ood/config/ood_portal.yml"}
rnode_uri: "/rnode"
host_regex: "[\\w.-]+\\.example\\.com"
```

Set `host_regex` to a pattern that matches the host names of your compute
nodes, as reported by `hostname` on the node. Then regenerate the portal
configuration and restart Apache:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
/opt/ood/ood-portal-generator/sbin/update_ood_portal
systemctl restart httpd
```

Skip this step if `rnode_uri` is already set. The Jupyter and RStudio apps
from the OOD documentation use the same setting.

## Step 5: Launch a session {#launch-a-session}

1. Sign in to OOD and open **Interactive Apps**, then **Positron**.
2. Leave the form at its defaults for the first session. The default request
   is one core, 2.5 GB of memory, and one hour.
3. Select **Launch**. OOD submits a Slurm job and shows the session card under
   **My Interactive Sessions**.
4. When the card changes to **Running**, select **Connect to Positron**.
   Positron opens in a new tab.

The first start takes longer than later starts, because Positron Server
unpacks its built-in extensions into `~/.positron-server` for that user.

## Step 6: Confirm it works {#confirm-it-works}

Run the [test checklist](test_checklist.qmd). It covers the R console, the
Python console, files, plots, the data explorer, and a clean session end.

## How it works

When a user selects **Launch**, OOD submits a Slurm job with the resources from
the form. On the compute node, the job:

1. Picks a free port and makes a random connection token.
2. Loads the module or adds `positron_server_dir/bin` to `PATH`.
3. Starts `positron-server` on that port with the token file, the license
   terms accepted, and telemetry off.
4. Waits up to 10 minutes for the port to open, then marks the session as
   running.

The **Connect to Positron** button opens `/rnode/<host>/<port>/?tkn=<token>`.
OOD proxies the request to the compute node, and Positron Server checks the
token on every request. Only the user who owns the session has the token.

Positron Server checks the license before it listens on the port. A missing,
expired, or altered license stops the session, and OOD reports a timeout.
[Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.qmd) shows what each failure looks like in
the session log.
